moves.spoken: A twenty-four-thirty-nine opponent. e4, and Black replies d5 — the Scandinavian.
Black recaptures with the queen, and the move is the knight to c3, hitting it with tempo.
The queen to d8 is one of the possible retreats.
The move here is of course d4, seizing the center, and Black develops the knight to f6.
The knight to f3, developing.
Black plays c6, and we bring the bishop out to c4, seeking the most active squares for our pieces.
b5 is already pretty weird.
The bishop steps back to b3.
I'm not sure what b5 achieves other than creating weaknesses. Black plays e6.
Let's complete our development and castle.
Black develops the bishop to e7. Now, where does the queen's bishop belong in these positions?
In my view the most active square is f4 — the bishop to f4 is a good move.
Black castles, and we slam the knight into e5 — and the bishop does a nice job keeping that knight stable.
Black plays the knight to d5. White is slightly better, and this is one of those moments where you just keep the tension.
So we drop the bishop back to g3, maintaining everything.
Black takes on c3, seemingly ruining my pawn structure.
We recapture, b takes c3 — and I'll explain during the game why this doubled structure isn't actually a problem.
On one hand it's doubled, but on the other we have a big mass of central pawns all defending each other. Black plays a5 and we answer a4.
Black plays the bishop to a6, creating an x-ray against my rook. How should we respond?
Simply the rook to e1 — and now you should immediately notice how loose Black's pawns on e6 and f7 are.
Black plays c5.
The knight takes on f7 — I play it pretty intuitively, because at the very least it's a rook for two pieces, and it hits the queen while stripping the defender of e6.
Black recaptures with the rook, and now the bishop takes on e6 — the defender is gone and the attack crashes through.
Black plays the bishop to b7. Notice the rook in the corner is undefended, which means our threats are just getting started.
Black resigns — a nice, clean game.
